nodes.summary: A mixing transformation $T$ of a probability space $(X, \mu)$ is ergodic. Indeed, if $E$ is a measurable set with $T^{-1} E = E$, then $T^{-n} E = E$ for every $n$, so the mixing property applied to $A = B = E$ gives hence $\mu(E) = \mu(E)^2$ and $\mu(E) \in \{0, 1\}$. Ergodicity in Mathlib (`Ergodic`) only needs to be checked on strictly invariant measurable sets, which is how the proof is organised.
nodes.title: Mixing implies ergodicity

nodes.summary: Let $(S, p)$ be a probability space. The Bernoulli scheme with distribution $p$ is the left shift $\sigma(x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots) = (x_1, x_2, \dots)$ on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$ with the product measure $p^{\mathbb{N}}$. It is mixing, whence ergodic.
nodes.title: Bernoulli shifts are mixing

nodes.summary: A measurable map $T$ of a measure space $(X, \mu)$ is *mixing* (strongly mixing) if it preserves $\mu$ and, for all measurable sets $A$ and $B$, For a probability measure this says that the event $T^{-n} B$, "the orbit is in $B$ at time $n$", becomes asymptotically independent of the event $A$. The measures take values in $[0, \infty]$; the notion is meant, as in the source, for probability-preserving maps.
nodes.title: Strong mixing

nodes.summary: If `T` is mixing then so is `T^[k]` for every `k ≥ 1`: the sequence `μ (A ∩ T^{-kn} B)` is a subsequence of `μ (A ∩ T^{-n} B)`.
nodes.title: Powers of a mixing map are mixing

The shift reads the next symbol

nodes.summary: The left shift on one-sided sequences, $\sigma(x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots) = (x_1, x_2, \dots)$ on $S^{\mathbb{N}}$: $(\sigma x)_n = x_{n+1}$ (the shift reads the next symbol). In Lean it is Mathlib's full shift by $1$ on configurations indexed by $\mathbb{N}$, `SymbolicDynamics.FullShift.shift 1`, under a short name; with a product measure $p^{\mathbb{N}}$ it is the Bernoulli scheme.
nodes.title: The one-sided left shift

nodes.summary: The left shift on bi-infinite sequences, $(\sigma x)_n = x_{n+1}$ on $S^{\mathbb{Z}}$. It is invertible, and with a product measure $p^{\mathbb{Z}}$ it is an invertible Bernoulli scheme, the setting of Ornstein's isomorphism theorem.
